messages.subject: mutate a subset in dplyr
messages.body_plain:
Hi, this sounds quite easy, but I couldn't find how to do it cleanly after searching the docs and the web.

I'm used to updating (or mutating) a subset of a tbl using data.table quite easily like this dt[cond_to_change == TRUE, col_to_change := val]
I tried doing something similar with dplyr, but had to resort to using ifelse, and it brings 2 problems
Sometimes the value can't be computed for that row (e.g., log of a neg number)
ifelse sometimes strips classes and is slow
Is there a dplyr way to do this cleanly? Something like a subset argument to mutate?

On Aug 1, 2014, at 12:25 PM, Juan Manuel Truppia wrote:

> Hi, this sounds quite easy, but I couldn't find how to do it cleanly after searching the docs and the web.
>
> I'm used to updating (or mutating) a subset of a tbl using data.table quite easily like this dt[cond_to_change == TRUE, col_to_change := val]

The `==TRUE` looks superfluous.

If one were working with dataframes wouldn't this be equivalent to:

df[ with(df, cond_to_change) & !is.na <http://is.na>(cond_to_change), col_to_change ] <- val

> I tried doing something similar with dplyr, but had to resort to using ifelse, and it brings 2 problems
> 	• Sometimes the value can't be computed for that row (e.g., log of a neg number)
> 	• ifelse sometimes strips classes and is slow
> Is there a dplyr way to do this cleanly? Something like a subset argument to mutate?

I remember a contribution by G.Grothendieck to SO in a question about implementing self-reference outside of data.table:

stackoverflow.com/questions/7768686/r-self-reference/7769296 <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/7768686/r-self-reference/7769296>

...  that suggestion led me to target subsets in what seemed to be an an elegant manner using an infix operator:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/7768686/r-self-reference/7769296#7769296

So playing around to see if this sort of think worked with data.tables:

 sel.cond.set.val <- function(dt, cond, target, val) {
   eval.parent(substitute(dt[cond, target := val])) }

 DT = data.table(x=rep(c("a","b","c"),each=3), y=c(1,3,6), v=1:9)

> DT
   x y v
1: a 1 1
2: a 3 2
3: a 6 3
4: b 1 4
5: b 3 5
6: b 6 6
7: c 1 7
8: c 3 8
9: c 6 9

 sel.cond.set.val(DT, x=="a", v, 10)
   x y  v
1: a 1 10
2: a 3 10
3: a 6 10
4: b 1  4
5: b 3  5
6: b 6  6
7: c 1  7
8: c 3  8
9: c 6  9

And it supports partial vector assignment (with a warning if 'val'-data overruns):

> sel.cond.set.val(DT, x=="a", v, 10:1)
   x y  v
1: a 1 10
2: a 3  9
3: a 6  8
4: b 1  4
5: b 3  5
6: b 6  6
7: c 1  7
8: c 3  8
9: c 6  9
Warning message:
In `[.data.table`(DT, x == "a", `:=`(v, 10:1)) :
  Supplied 10 items to be assigned to 3 items of column 'v' (7 unused)

That warning message made it look like I was merely rearranging a few symbols in the function call.

I don't think that violates any of the data.table conventions that would make copies. My understanding of the conventions of dplyr are pretty weak. I've formed the apparently incorrect opinion that the goal of dplyr was to convert to a left-to-right passage of data through infix operators, but I guess there aren't filters that modify data.tables or dataframes through input. It's a bit unclear what sort of syntax would be desired. I guess this is further incentive to actually learn dplyr.

Reading the Intro blog at RStudio mades me wonder if dplyr is focused only on dataframes? ( I thought it was being designed to work with data.tables, but the intro made me think not.)

I tried coming up with a version that could detect DT vs DF

sel.cond.set.val <- function(dobj, cond, col, val) { if(is.data.table(dobj)){
  eval.parent(substitute(dobj[cond, col := val])) } else{
eval.parent(substitute( dobj[ with(dobj, cond) , col ] <- val)) }}

But my understanding is that the use of `with` may pose hidden dangers that I don't fully understand.

--

David Winsemius
Alameda, CA, USA

Use `do` to subset to the variables you want, calculate the sum, and return the result as a data frame. According to the help for `do`, the result must always be a data frame.

mydf %>%
  group_by(vara) %>%
  do(subset(., select = varshort) %>% sum %>% data.frame(sss = .))

If you don't need to set the variable name (`sss`), then you can replace `data.frame(sss = .)` with `data.frame`.

the p-value for the test.

method

library(plyr)

df1 <- data.frame(
    entity = rep(c("A","B","C"),each = 3),
    date1 = c(
        ymd("2014-01-02"),  # A
        ymd("2014-01-07"),
        ymd("2014-01-15"),
        ymd("2014-01-04"),  # B
        ymd("2014-01-09"),
        ymd("2014-01-13"),

        ymd("2014-01-08"),

        ymd("2014-01-06"),  # A
        ymd("2014-01-14"),
        ymd("2014-01-20"),
        ymd("2014-01-08"),  # B
        ymd("2014-01-12"),
        ymd("2014-01-19"),
        ymd("2014-01-07"),  # C
        ymd("2014-01-13"),
        ymd("2014-01-21")))
df1 <- mutate(df1, date1=round_date(date1,'day'),date2=round_date(date2,'day'))
df2 <- data.frame(
    datestamp = ymd("2014-01-01")+days(0:22),
    data = 1:23)
df1 <- mutate(df1, date1adj = round_date(date1 - days(1), 'day'),
              date2adj = round_date(date2 - days(1), 'day'))

## The Query:
q3b <- sqldf("select df1.entity, df1.date1, df1.date2,
              (select sum(data) from df2 where datestamp between df1.date1adj and df1.date2)
              as periodsums from df1")

Is there a reasonable way to express that in dplyr (or even plyr)?  Is it likely to be faster?  My real df1 has over 100,000 rows.

Thanks,

Bill

Hi Grant,

I have some inkling about how to solve this problem - I think dplyr
needs a cross_join(). The above example is a bit complicated because
it also uses subquery, but I think the following would be equivalent:

df2 %>%
  full_join(df1) %>%
  group_by(entity) %>%
  filter(between(datestamp, date1adj, date2)) %>%
  summarise(periodsums = sum(data))

But it's not clear to me yet if this is expressive enough.

A implementation for local data frames will also be relatively tough,
since cross_join() should ideally work lazily, so that it doesn't have
to realise the full cartesian product.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Hadley, thanks for looking into this.

I think a cross join would be a great addition to dplyr.  There certainly are cases where I use sqldf because I don't know how to do a cross join in dplyr.  However, like you I'm not sure it's sufficient to span the space of what people want.  In particular, when joining on an inequality condition, I think it's very common to want a left join methodology.  This means any rows in the left dataset for which there are no rows in the right table matching the inequality would appear in the final join, but have NA in the columns that should come from the right dataset.  If one implements this by cross joining and then filtering, I don't think there will be any rows with NA on the right hand side.  It would be like an inner join with inequality conditions.

Let's step away from the example with a subquery to glance at a simpler example similar to some recent code of mine.  Suppose I wanted to add every return from Returns for each fund month starting before a 3 month gap and up to a year before that.

  FundsWithReturns <- sqldf('select d1.*, d2.ReturnRf
                             from FundMonths d1 left join Returns d2
                             on d1.FundID = d2.FundID
                             and d1.yearmonth - 3 > d2.gmonth
                             and d1.yearmonth - 3 - 12 <= d2.gmonth')

It would also be nice to aggregate these returns in the same query, but in the do-one-thing-well spirit of dplyr it likely makes sense to do this join and then aggregate with a summarize() command.  Optimally, the join command would look like this

   FundsWithReturns <- left_join(FundMonths, Returns, FundID == FundID, yearmonth > gmonth +3, yearmonth <= gmonth + 3 +12)

Followed by a select() command if I wanted to drop out unwanted columns added from Returns. For backward compatibility and brevity, this could be abbreviated

   FundsWithReturns <- left_join(FundMonths, Returns, FundID, yearmonth > gmonth +3, yearmonth <= gmonth + 3 +12)

Basically any argument after the first two would be either equality or inequality with the left hand side of the conditional being variables from the left hand dataset and right hand stuff from the right hand.  If no conditional is specified, equality of a variable with the same name in both datasets is assumed.  This would also solve people's complaints who want to join on variables that are equal but do not have the same name in both datasets.  [Of course a rename() verb is also a great idea.  I have heard that suggestion around.]

Notice that every row from FundMonths here would be included, even if there is no data in the Returns dataset matching the three specified merge conditions.  You'd just have an NA in the resulting ReturnRf column in that case.

I don't know how the internals of the current join methodology work but it seems like making the matching conditions include the possibility of inequalities and simple transformations (or perhaps any transformation that can be computed using only information from one row in each table) would be easier than writing a cross join that intelligently knows which rows to compute based on a subsequent filter.  You are the expert, of course, so you would know better than me.

What do you think?

Thanks again for the incredibly important and valuable contribution you make to the R world.
Grant

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rachael,

The problem is this:

sst=mean(SST, na.rm=TRUE),
sstSD=sd(sst, na.rm=TRUE)

You're overwriting the original sst variable with it's mean, then
trying to create the standard deviation of one number.

You might also want to look at summarise_each which makes this sort of
thing easier:

hab %>%
  group_by(year, eco, id) %>%

  summarize_each(
    funs(mean = mean(., na.rm = TRUE), sd = sd(., na.rm = TRUE)),
    sst, depth, slope, ssh, eke, hill, disttocenter, windsp
  )

Hadley
